metadata.title: How effective is the professional development in which teachers typically participate? Quasi-experimental analyses of effects on student achievement based on TIMSS 2003-2019

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS’s two-stage clustered sampling design (schools sampled first, then classes within schools) and therefore applies complex survey adjustments. For descriptive statistics, it uses teacher-level probability weights and jackknife repeated replication (JRR) to compute means and standard errors, following TIMSS & PIRLS International Study Center recommendations. For the main PD-effect models, it uses sampling weights that give each country equal weight (senwgt) so that differences in country sample sizes do not drive results, and it uses clustered standard errors to account for within-school clustering (implemented via Stata 17 and Mplus 8.8). The analytic sample is restricted to OECD countries and further excludes specific OECD countries in particular cycles that failed TIMSS sample guidelines; these restrictions are part of the effective weighting target population.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Data are drawn from TIMSS 2003, 2007, 2011, 2015, and 2019 cycles, restricted to OECD countries (with three OECD countries excluded in specific cycles for failing TIMSS sample guidelines). The study includes grade four and grade eight mathematics and science assessments. For the within-student between-subjects fixed-effects approach, each student must have one value per subject area; when students are taught by more than one teacher in a subject, the study averages (or sums for instruction time) teacher-linked variables to obtain one value per subject area. The main model uses all available students under this averaging strategy, and a sensitivity analysis excludes students taught by more than one teacher in each subject area.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Main model (with student fixed effects, all controls): Effect = -0.017 SD (p = 0.002). Sensitivity: without student fixed effects, effect is positive (e.g., Effect = 0.090 SD, p < 0.001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2003-2019 pooled data for Grade 4 mathematics and science, the study leveraged teachers’ mathematics/science PD participation (latent PD index) together with socioeconomic and teacher controls to estimate student achievement differences within students across subjects, finding that PD effects are small and negative (about -0.017 SD, p = 0.002) once student fixed effects are included. This indicates that typical mathematics/science PD participation, as measured in TIMSS, is not translating into meaningful short-run achievement gains and may even coincide with slight declines, suggesting policymakers should be cautious about assuming PD participation alone improves learning.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Main model (with student fixed effects, all controls): Effect = -0.020 SD (p = 0.010). Without student fixed effects, effects are positive (e.g., Effect = 0.132 SD, p < 0.001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2003-2019 pooled data for Grade 8 mathematics and science, the study leveraged teachers’ mathematics/science PD participation (latent PD index) with socioeconomic and teacher controls in a within-student between-subjects fixed-effects framework, finding that PD effects are small and negative (about -0.020 SD, p = 0.010) when student fixed effects are included. This indicates that typical PD participation is unlikely to produce substantial achievement improvements in the short run for Grade 8 students, and that PD policies may need stronger attention to PD quality and implementation rather than participation rates.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses TIMSS 2003, 2007, 2011, 2015, and 2019 nationally representative data from OECD countries, analyzing grade 4 and grade 8 mathematics and science achievement in a within-student between-subjects fixed-effects design. Teachers’ typical PD participation is measured from teacher questionnaires across five PD topics (content, pedagogy, curriculum, IT integration, assessment), recoded into dummy indicators and summarized as a latent PD participation variable. Student achievement is modeled using TIMSS plausible values (five PVs per student) with TYPE=IMPUTATION in Mplus, and missing data are handled via full information maximum likelihood (FIML). Across cycles, the main model estimates PD effects close to zero and slightly negative: for grade 4, about -0.017 SD (p=0.002), and for grade 8, about -0.020 SD (p=0.010) after including student fixed effects and controls. The paper also finds heterogeneity, with negative effects concentrated among higher-achieving students, and it emphasizes that these are quasi-experimental observational estimates where causality cannot be fully guaranteed despite robustness checks.
